Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- Heavy rains smashed through a dam near Indonesia's capital Friday, unleashing a torrent of water that plowed into hundreds of homes and killed at least 52 people in what some survivors described as a suburban "tsunami." Members of a search and rescue team look for bodies around upended trees and vehicles near  Jakarta Friday. Sleeping residents were taken by surprise by the powerful flash flood as it crashed through Jakarta's crowded Cirendeu suburb, in the early hours of the morning. Rescue crews suspended their search for survivors overnight Friday evening, the National Disaster Coordination Agency said. The agency put the death toll at 52 with 17 missing. It said 33 people were injured and 1,490 left homeless. The Indonesian Health Ministry put the death toll higher at 58 people. After the deluge, drenched, injured and shivering survivors took refuge on the rooftops of their homes as rescuers in rubber boats struggled to reach them. Social affairs spokesman official Mardjito, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said relief efforts were being hampered by debris from the dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he said. Pictures from the scene showed the pulverized ruins of wooden buildings emerging as brown muddied waters subside.  Watch scenes of the flood devastation » . Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently on the campaign trail ahead of elections later this year, said he had ordered senior ministers to visit the scene of the disaster. "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty," he said, according to the official Antara news agency. The rain obliterated a 255-meter-long section of the dam at around 4 am local time, releasing a wall of water from the 20-hectare lake that some survivors said reminded them of the tsunami that hit Indonesia in 2004. "They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam's lake," Antara said. Survivors told stories of dead relatives and harrowing brushes with death as they struggled to escape rising waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told the AFP news agency that she escaped with her husband and two daughters after they saw rising water reach the door of their stilt house. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. "I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she said, showing cuts and scratches on her arms." Floods from heavy rains are an annual occurrence around Jakarta, a low lying city on the northern coast of Java island, where poor infrastructure often results in polluted canals and rivers spilling their banks and spilling into thousands of homes. In 2007, 38 people were killed and 430,000 forced from their homes when storm waters three meters deep in some places swamped 75 percent of the capital, which is home to about 9 million people. With poor sanitation and a hot and humid climate, the risk of water-borne diseases is usually a major concern following floods in the city, where mosquito-transmitted malaria is also a threat. CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- A dam close to Indonesia's capital gave way under the force of intense rainfall on Friday, sending a surge of water crashing into hundreds of homes and claiming at least 52 lives in an event some survivors compared to a "tsunami" hitting their neighborhood. Search and rescue personnel combed through debris, uprooted trees, and overturned vehicles near Jakarta looking for victims. The flash flood struck without warning during the early morning hours, catching residents of Jakarta's densely populated Cirendeu suburb while they slept. According to the National Disaster Coordination Agency, search operations for survivors were halted overnight on Friday. The agency reported 52 confirmed deaths, 17 people still unaccounted for, 33 injuries, and 1,490 individuals displaced from their homes. However, Indonesia's Health Ministry cited a higher death count of 58.

Following the disaster, soaked, wounded, and cold survivors sought safety atop their rooftops while rescue teams in rubber dinghies fought to reach them. Mardjito, a spokesman for social affairs who—like many Indonesians—uses a single name, explained that relief operations were being slowed by debris scattered from the collapsed dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he explained. Images from the disaster zone revealed shattered wooden structures emerging as the murky brown floodwaters receded.

Watch scenes of the flood devastation »

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently campaigning for this year's upcoming elections, announced that he had directed top ministers to travel to the disaster site. According to the state-run Antara news agency, he stated, "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty."

The torrential rain destroyed a 255-meter stretch of the dam around 4 a.m. local time, unleashing floodwaters from the 20-hectare reservoir that some witnesses likened to the devastating 2004 tsunami that struck Indonesia. Antara reported that survivors described hearing thunderous rumbling similar to a major earthquake, only later realizing the noise came from water bursting out of the dam's reservoir.

Survivors recounted losing relatives and narrowly escaping death as they fled the surging waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old homemaker, told AFP that she fled with her husband and two daughters after watching floodwater rise to the entrance of their elevated home. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she recounted, displaying cuts and scrapes on her arms.

Seasonal flooding from heavy rains regularly plagues Jakarta, a low-elevation city situated on Java's northern shoreline, where inadequate infrastructure frequently causes contaminated waterways and rivers to overflow, inundating thousands of residences. Back in 2007, floodwaters reaching three meters deep submerged 75 percent of the capital—home to roughly 9 million people—killing 38 individuals and displacing 430,000 residents. Given the city's poor sanitation systems and humid tropical climate, health officials typically worry about waterborne illness outbreaks following major floods, alongside the ongoing threat of mosquito-borne malaria.

CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

# Dam Collapse Near Jakarta Kills Dozens in Flash Flood Disaster

A dam located on the outskirts of Jakarta gave way on Friday following days of torrential rainfall, unleashing a catastrophic wall of water that tore through hundreds of homes in nearby communities. The disaster has claimed the lives of at least 52 people, according to official government reports, with fears that the death toll could continue to rise as search and rescue operations proceed.

## Survivors Describe Scene of Terror

Those who managed to escape the deluge described the experience in harrowing terms, with many drawing comparisons to the devastating 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami that killed hundreds of thousands across Indonesia and other coastal nations. Survivors recounted how the flood arrived with little warning, transforming from a distant rumble into a powerful surge of water that swept away everything in its path within moments. The sudden nature of the collapse left residents with virtually no time to gather belongings or, in many tragic cases, to escape at all before the torrent overwhelmed their homes.

## Conflicting Casualty Figures

Discrepancies have emerged between government agencies regarding the exact human toll of the disaster. The National Disaster Coordination Agency, the primary body responsible for tracking such emergencies, reported that 52 people had died, with an additional 17 individuals still listed as missing. The agency also documented 33 people injured in the flooding, while a staggering 1,490 residents have been left homeless, their houses either destroyed or rendered uninhabitable by the flood's force.

However, the Health Ministry offered a different account of the casualties, placing the death toll at 58—six higher than the figure cited by the disaster agency. Such discrepancies are not uncommon in the immediate aftermath of large-scale disasters, when information from multiple sources is still being verified and consolidated.

## Rescue Operations Hindered by Debris

Emergency response teams faced significant obstacles in their efforts to locate and rescue survivors. Thick layers of mud combined with debris from destroyed structures created treacherous conditions that slowed the pace of rescue operations considerably. In many areas, rescue workers were forced to abandon conventional means of transport and instead relied on rubber boats to navigate the flooded terrain, searching for residents who had climbed onto rooftops to escape the rising waters.

Despite the urgency of the situation, deteriorating visibility and safety concerns eventually compelled authorities to suspend search efforts as night fell. Rescue teams indicated they would resume their work at first light, though concerns remained high for those still unaccounted for, particularly given the conditions that any survivors might be enduring overnight.

## Political Response Amid Election Campaign

The disaster has prompted a swift response from Indonesia's highest levels of government. President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, who is currently in the midst of an election campaign, moved quickly to address the tragedy despite his political commitments. The president issued directives to senior members of his cabinet, instructing them to travel to the affected area personally to assess the damage and coordinate the government's response to the crisis.

In a public statement, President Yudhoyono extended his condolences to the families who had lost loved ones in the disaster, acknowledging the scale of the tragedy that had befallen the community. His decision to dispatch top ministers to the scene, even as he continues his campaign activities, signals the government's recognition of the severity of the situation and the political importance of demonstrating an effective disaster response.

As recovery efforts continue, authorities face the dual challenge of locating remaining survivors while beginning the broader process of supporting displaced families and assessing the long-term infrastructure and public safety implications of the dam's failure.

# Flash Floods Kill Dozens After Dam Collapse Near Jakarta

## Emergency crews search for survivors as death toll continues to rise

**JAKARTA, Indonesia** — At least 47 people are dead and dozens more are missing after a dam collapsed in the hills south of Jakarta early Tuesday morning, sending a wall of water crashing through several densely populated villages while residents slept.

The Katulampa auxiliary dam, part of a water management system that regulates flow from the Ciliwung River into the capital, gave way around 3:15 a.m. local time following days of unusually heavy monsoon rains, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB).

"The water came so fast there was no time to run," said Sutrisno, a 52-year-old rice farmer who lost his home in the village of Cisarua, one of the hardest-hit areas. Like many Indonesians, he goes by one name. "I heard a sound like thunder, but it did not stop. I grabbed my wife and we climbed onto the roof. We watched our neighbors' houses disappear."

Sutrisno's family survived, but he said at least three neighbors, including a young child, were swept away.

## Scenes of devastation

Aerial footage released by the Indonesian military showed entire neighborhoods submerged, with only rooftops and treetops visible above the muddy floodwaters. Cars, motorbikes and livestock were seen tangled in debris fields that stretched for more than a mile downstream.

Rina Wijaya, 34, described a frantic scramble to save her three children after floodwaters breached the walls of her home in Bogor Regency.

"My youngest is only two years old," she said, sitting outside a temporary shelter set up in a local mosque, wrapped in a donated blanket. "I put him on my shoulders and we waded through water up to my chest. I do not know how we survived. Others were not so lucky."

Local officials say the death toll is expected to rise as search teams reach more remote areas that were cut off by destroyed roads and bridges. More than 60 people remain unaccounted for, according to the latest BNPB figures, though officials cautioned that number is fluid as families continue to report missing relatives.

More than 5,000 residents have been displaced and are currently housed in emergency shelters, schools and mosques across the region.

## Search and rescue operations underway

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency (BASARNAS) has deployed over 800 personnel, along with military units, to the affected areas. Divers are searching submerged homes and vehicles, while helicopters have been used to airlift stranded residents from rooftops.

"Our priority right now is locating survivors," said BASARNAS spokesperson Ahmad Yani. "But we are also recovering bodies, and unfortunately we expect to find more in the coming days as the water recedes."

Heavy machinery has been brought in to clear debris blocking access roads, though officials say some villages remain reachable only by boat or on foot.

## Government response and questions over dam safety

President Prabowo Subianto declared the flooding a national disaster Tuesday afternoon and pledged full government support for relief efforts, including emergency funding for rebuilding infrastructure and compensating families who lost homes.

"This is a tragedy that has struck our nation, and we will not abandon the people of Bogor and the surrounding areas," Prabowo said in a televised address. "I have ordered all relevant ministries to mobilize resources immediately."

The president also ordered an investigation into the cause of the dam's failure, amid growing public criticism over the condition of the decades-old structure. Local environmental groups have warned for years that aging flood-control infrastructure around Jakarta was inadequately maintained and ill-equipped to handle the increasingly intense rainfall linked to climate change.

Indonesia's Public Works Ministry said the dam had undergone an inspection roughly 18 months ago but disputed claims from some residents that visible cracks had been reported to local authorities in the weeks before the collapse.

"We take these allegations seriously, and they will be part of the official investigation," said ministry spokesperson Dedi Kurniawan. "Our first priority right now is saving lives."

## A pattern of vulnerability

Jakarta and its surrounding areas have long struggled with flooding, worsened by rapid urbanization, deforestation in upstream hill regions, and a rainy season that experts say has become more erratic due to climate change. Greater Jakarta is home to more than 30 million people, many of them in flood-prone lowland areas.

Environmental researcher Dwi Hartanto, of the University of Indonesia, said Tuesday's disaster should serve as a wake-up call.

"This is not simply a natural disaster — it is the result of decades of underinvestment in aging infrastructure combined with the increasing intensity of storms we're seeing across the region," Hartanto said. "Unless serious reforms are made, we will see this happen again."

For survivors like Rina Wijaya, the search for accountability feels secondary to the immediate task of rebuilding.

"I don't know if we will ever go back," she said, glancing toward her two older children playing quietly nearby. "Everything we had is gone. I am just grateful we are alive."

---

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as more information becomes available.*

# Flash Floods Devastate Jakarta Suburbs After Dam Failure; Death Toll Rises as Rescuers Race Against Time

**BEKASI, Indonesia** — A catastrophic dam failure triggered flash flooding across densely populated suburbs east of Jakarta early Tuesday, killing at least 47 people and displacing thousands, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB). Officials warned the death toll could climb as search teams continue combing through debris-choked neighborhoods.

The disaster began around 3:00 a.m. local time when heavy monsoon rains, which had battered the region for nearly 36 hours, overwhelmed the aging Cileungsi retention dam. Structural engineers say a section of the earthen embankment gave way under pressure, sending a wall of water estimated at nearly three meters high surging through the Bekasi and Bogor regencies within minutes.

## "There Was No Time to Run"

Survivors described scenes of chaos as water tore through homes while residents slept. "We heard a roar like thunder, and then the water was already at our door," said Siti Rahayu, 34, a mother of three who escaped to a rooftop with her children before being rescued by boat hours later. "There was no warning. No siren. Nothing."

Local officials have acknowledged that early warning systems for the dam had not been upgraded since installation over two decades ago, raising questions about infrastructure oversight in one of the world's most flood-prone metropolitan areas.

## Rescue Operations Underway

More than 3,500 personnel from the Indonesian military, national search and rescue agency (Basarnas), and volunteer groups have been deployed to affected areas. Rescue workers using rubber boats and helicopters have pulled hundreds of survivors from rooftops and trees, while search dogs comb through collapsed structures for the missing.

"Our priority right now is locating survivors trapped in debris and reaching isolated pockets that vehicles cannot access," said Basarnas spokesperson Bambang Sutrisno. Temporary shelters have been established in nearby school buildings and mosques, though officials say supplies of clean water and medical aid remain critically limited.

Hospitals in Bekasi have reported an influx of patients suffering from injuries, hypothermia, and waterborne illness, with several clinics reaching capacity by midday Tuesday.

## Echoes of 2004

For many older residents, the scale of destruction has revived painful memories of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which killed over 230,000 people across the region, including tens of thousands in Indonesia's Aceh province. While Tuesday's disaster is far smaller in scope, disaster response experts note unsettling parallels — the suddenness of the water's arrival, the failure of early warning infrastructure, and the vulnerability of low-lying communities built close to water systems.

"This wasn't an earthquake or an ocean wave, but the speed and force were comparable to what we saw in 2004," said Dr. Ratna Dewi, a disaster risk specialist at the University of Indonesia. "It's a sobering reminder that infrastructure failures can produce tsunami-like devastation in a matter of minutes."

## Calls for Accountability

President Joko Widodo's office has ordered an immediate investigation into the dam's structural integrity and maintenance history, with early reports suggesting warnings about erosion along the embankment had been flagged by engineers as far back as 2019 but never fully addressed.

"This tragedy should never have happened," said opposition lawmaker Anies Baswedan, calling for a full audit of flood infrastructure across Greater Jakarta. "We are once again seeing preventable loss of life due to neglected warning systems and aging infrastructure."

As floodwaters begin to recede in some areas, authorities have shifted focus toward recovery efforts, though officials caution that additional rainfall forecast for later this week could further complicate search operations and risk renewed flooding.

The government has pledged emergency housing and financial assistance for displaced families, though many residents say they fear it will be months, if not years, before their communities recover.

---

**Dam Collapse Unleashes Deadly Floods Across Jakarta Suburbs, Dozens Missing**

*By CNN Staff*

**JAKARTA, Indonesia** — Torrential monsoon rains triggered the catastrophic failure of the Katulampa auxiliary dam early Tuesday morning, sending a wall of water crashing through densely populated districts south of Jakarta and leaving at least 27 people dead, dozens missing, and thousands displaced, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB).

The dam, part of a flood-control network built decades ago to protect the capital from seasonal flooding, gave way around 3:15 a.m. local time after more than 300 millimeters of rain fell in under 18 hours — nearly triple the average for this time of year. Officials say the reservoir had already reached critical capacity before the structure's earthen embankment collapsed, releasing an estimated 40 million cubic meters of water downstream.

**"We heard a sound like thunder, but it didn't stop"**

Survivors described a terrifying, sudden onslaught that gave residents little time to escape.

"We heard a sound like thunder, but it didn't stop," said Siti Rahayu, 42, a mother of three from the hard-hit Bogor regency. "Then the water was at my chest. I grabbed my children and we climbed to the roof. We stayed there for six hours until a rescue boat came."

Another resident, Andi Kurniawan, recounted losing his motorcycle repair shop and nearly his life. "The wall of water came so fast. I climbed a mango tree with my neighbor's baby in my arms. I have never been so afraid."

Rescue teams using inflatable boats and helicopters have been working since dawn to reach stranded families, many trapped on rooftops or in trees. Indonesia's Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) said more than 4,000 personnel, including military units, have been deployed.

**A history of vulnerability**

Tuesday's disaster reignites long-standing concerns about Jakarta's flood infrastructure, much of which dates back to the Dutch colonial era and has struggled to keep pace with the city's rapid urbanization and sinking terrain — parts of North Jakarta are sinking up to 25 centimeters per year due to groundwater extraction.

Jakarta has faced repeated catastrophic flooding in recent decades:

- In **2007**, floods submerged nearly 70% of the city, killed dozens, and displaced hundreds of thousands.
- The **2013** floods breached a major canal wall in the city center, paralyzing the business district and forcing evacuations from the presidential palace grounds.
- Most recently, **New Year's flooding in 2020** brought the heaviest rainfall in over two decades, killing at least 60 people and displacing nearly 400,000 residents.

Experts have long warned that Jakarta's flood defenses — including dams, canals, and pumping stations — are outdated and underfunded relative to the scale of the threat.

"This is a symptom of a much larger crisis," said Dr. Amara Wibowo, a hydrologist at the University of Indonesia. "Jakarta sits on a floodplain, is sinking, and faces increasingly erratic rainfall due to climate change. Infrastructure built for the 20th century cannot handle 21st-century storms."

**Government response**

President Joko Widodo's successor, addressing the nation Tuesday afternoon, pledged emergency funding for reconstruction and vowed to "urgently accelerate" the long-delayed relocation of the capital to Nusantara on Borneo — a project partly justified by Jakarta's chronic flooding and sinking crisis.

Meteorologists warn that more heavy rain is expected through the week, raising fears of further flooding and potential landslides in hillside areas already saturated by days of downpours.

Emergency shelters have been set up in mosques, schools, and community centers across Bogor and South Jakarta, though officials say supplies of clean water and medical aid remain limited.

As floodwaters begin to recede in some areas, residents are left to assess the wreckage — collapsed homes, destroyed roads, and, for many families, an uncertain path to rebuilding lives upended in a matter of hours.

*CNN's coverage of this developing story will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Dam Collapse Near Jakarta Kills Dozens, Triggers Search for Missing

**JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP)** — A dam collapsed following days of torrential rain on the outskirts of Jakarta early Thursday, unleashing a wall of water and mud through several densely populated villages and killing at least 27 people, officials said.

The collapse of the Cimahi Dam, located roughly 20 miles southeast of the Indonesian capital, sent floodwaters surging through at least four villages while most residents were asleep, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB).

Agency spokesperson Abdul Muhari said the death toll was expected to rise as search-and-rescue teams continued combing through debris fields Thursday afternoon. At least 43 people were injured, several critically, and were being treated at hospitals in Bogor and Depok, officials said. Another 19 people remained unaccounted for as of Thursday evening.

"We are racing against time," Muhari told reporters at a press briefing. "Conditions on the ground remain difficult, with mud several meters deep in some areas and continued rainfall hampering rescue operations."

More than 1,200 people have been displaced and are currently sheltering in emergency centers set up at nearby mosques, schools and a sports complex, according to local disaster officials. Search teams, aided by heavy machinery, sniffer dogs and drones, were working to reach areas still cut off by debris and collapsed roadways.

Video footage circulating on social media showed the moment the earthen dam gave way, sending a torrent of brown water through nearby rice paddies and residential streets. Witnesses described hearing a loud crack before the flood arrived with little warning.

"There was no time to save anything. We just ran," said Suryani, a 45-year-old resident of Ciseeng village who like many Indonesians goes by one name. She said she lost her home and was still searching for her elderly mother, who was not among those confirmed dead or accounted for at shelters.

President Prabowo Subianto, who took office last year, visited the disaster site Thursday afternoon and pledged full government support for recovery efforts.

"My deepest condolences go out to the families who have lost loved ones in this tragedy," Prabowo said during a brief statement to reporters. "I have ordered all relevant ministries and agencies to mobilize every possible resource for search, rescue and recovery. We will also conduct a full investigation into the cause of this collapse to ensure such a disaster never happens again."

The president announced that the government would provide financial assistance to affected families and ordered an immediate inspection of dams and water infrastructure across the greater Jakarta region, citing concerns about aging infrastructure amid increasingly severe seasonal rains.

The Public Works and Housing Ministry said the dam, built in the 1980s, had undergone routine inspections but acknowledged that unusually heavy rainfall in recent days — reportedly the heaviest in over a decade for the region — may have overwhelmed its capacity.

Indonesia, an archipelago nation of more than 270 million people, regularly experiences deadly flooding and landslides during its rainy season, which typically runs from November to March. Rapid urban development and deforestation in watershed areas have been cited by environmental groups as factors that worsen flooding risks nationwide.

The Indonesian Red Cross said it was deploying additional personnel and medical supplies to the region, while the World Health Organization's Indonesia office said it was monitoring the situation for potential public health concerns, including waterborne disease risks in shelters.

Rescue operations were expected to continue through the night, with authorities warning residents in low-lying areas downstream to remain on alert for possible additional flooding.

This is a developing story and will be updated.
